title: Replication
subtitle: Use database copies for read capacity and fault tolerance while managing lag and failover
objectives: Explain what replication scales and what it doesn't
Describe single-leader replication and the synchronous/asynchronous choice
Recognize replication lag bugs and the routing fixes for them
Reason about failover: lost writes, split brain, and choosing which mistake to make

exercises.title: Replication maintains database copies on multiple machines
exercises.body: A primary copy records each write and sends an ordered change stream to replicas. Replicas replay those changes to maintain the same dataset and can answer read requests. Adding replicas distributes read work and provides a promotion candidate if the primary machine fails.
exercises.note: A replica is a changing copy, so asynchronous replay can expose older data. It also replicates accidental deletes and therefore does not replace a backup.

exercises.prompt: One leader receives 2,000 writes/s and 8,000 reads/s, exceeding its 6,000 req/s capacity. Route reads to two replicas.
exercises.afterStatus: LEADER LOAD · 2,000 / 6,000 req/s · replicas serve 4,000 reads/s each
exercises.result: Read traffic moved off the write authority
exercises.why: Read replicas increase read capacity by serving copies of the leader's data. Asynchronous replication can make those reads stale, so operations requiring current data may still need the leader or a caught-up replica.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the system for this case: One leader receives 2,000 writes/s and 8,000 reads/s, exceeding its 6,000 req/s capacity. Route reads to two replicas. Place Leader, Replica A, Replica B. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Application → Leader; Leader → Replica A; Leader → Replica B; Application → Replica A; Application → Replica B. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Read replicas increase read capacity by serving copies of the leader's data. Asynchronous replication can make those reads stale, so operations requiring current data may still need the leader or a caught-up replica.

exercises.prompt: Your app does 100 reads for every write, and your single database is drowning in reads. What's the structural fix?
choices: Add copies (replicas) that serve reads, leaving the original to handle writes
exercises.why: Read replicas can execute read-only queries using copies of the leader's data, distributing the 100-to-1 read load across machines. Writes still pass through the leader and must be replicated, so this improves capacity only while reads are the limiting workload and acceptable reads may use replicas.

exercises.prompt: The second reason to keep copies: your database machine dies at 3am. What does having a replica let you do?
choices: Nothing — you still restore from backup
Promote a replica to take over, so you stay online instead of waiting on a restore
Recover data faster from the dead disk
exercises.why: A healthy replica has an already-materialized copy and can be promoted after failure detection and safety checks, reducing recovery time compared with restoring a full backup. Replication also copies accidental deletes and corruption, so point-in-time backups remain necessary for logical recovery.

exercises.prompt: In the single-leader, full-replica design shown, what does adding followers buy you? Select all.
choices: Serving users from a geographically closer copy
exercises.why: Replicas can serve reads, provide promotion candidates after failure, and place readable copies nearer users. In single-leader replication, every logical write is accepted by the leader and replayed by followers, so adding full replicas does not divide write work or dataset size.

exercises.prompt: In this single-leader, full-replica design, adding followers scales ______ without dividing the leader's write stream.
exercises.why: A read-only query can be distributed among replicas that meet its freshness requirement. Each follower must still apply the leader's complete ordered write stream, so replication increases read-serving capacity without partitioning write throughput.

exercises.prompt: A user just changed an address on the leader. Which routing decisions match their freshness requirements? Select all.
choices: Send the immediate confirmation read to the leader for fresh state
Send a stale-tolerant analytics query to a follower
Prefer the most caught-up eligible follower as a failover candidate
Send a must-be-fresh read to any follower without checking its replay position
exercises.why: The leader has the acknowledged change, while an asynchronous follower may still be behind, so the immediate fresh read goes to the leader. Stale-tolerant analytics can use followers, and a failover candidate should be caught up enough for the loss policy. A follower read needs a protocol freshness check or a stated staleness allowance; routing to an arbitrary follower does not promise current state.

exercises.prompt: When are full-copy followers behind one leader the wrong scaling tool?
choices: When you have lots of reads
When writes are your bottleneck, or your dataset no longer fits on one machine
When users are spread across regions
exercises.why: In this full-copy single-leader design, every replica contains the dataset and replays the complete write stream, so followers cannot divide that leader's write bottleneck or shrink per-node data. Partitioned and some multi-leader systems can distribute accepted writes, but that is a different architecture with added coordination.

exercises.title: Single-leader replication gives one node authority to order writes
exercises.body: Clients send writes to the *leader*. The leader records them in a replication log with a defined order, and *followers* apply that log in the same order. Reads may use followers. Routing all writes through one authority prevents concurrent replicas from independently ordering conflicting updates.
exercises.note: The leader limits write throughput. After it fails, the system must promote one follower and fence the old leader before accepting writes safely.

exercises.prompt: One database handles 8,000 writes/s and 30,000 read/s. Writes fit, but total load does not. Route read-only traffic to three followers.
choices: Send writes to every follower independently
choiceFeedback: Followers add read-serving capacity while the leader remains the write authority.
Writes already fit; sharding introduces partitioning complexity without targeting the measured read bottleneck.
Independent multi-leader writes create conflict handling and do not preserve the stated single write authority.
exercises.result: Read capacity increased without splitting the write authority
exercises.why: Followers replay the leader's writes and can serve read-only queries, adding read capacity. Asynchronous followers can lag, so operations requiring fresh or read-your-writes data may need leader routing or a consistency mechanism.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: One database handles 8,000 writes/s and 30,000 read/s. Writes fit, but total load does not. Route read-only traffic to three followers. Place Leader, 3 followers. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Application → Leader; Application → 3 followers; Leader → 3 followers. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Followers replay the leader's writes and can serve read-only queries, adding read capacity. Asynchronous followers can lag, so operations requiring fresh or read-your-writes data may need leader routing or a consistency mechanism.

exercises.prompt: Suppose any copy could accept writes. What breaks?
choices: Two copies could accept conflicting writes to the same row, and there'd be no single right answer
The copies would run out of disk
exercises.why: If two copies independently accept writes to the same row during a delay or partition, their logs can contain incompatible values and orders. A single leader establishes one authoritative write order, avoiding conflict resolution on the normal write path.

exercises.prompt: Match each piece of single-leader replication to its role.

pairs.right: The only copy that accepts writes
A read-only copy kept in sync
The stream of changes the leader ships
Promoting a follower when the leader dies

exercises.why: The leader serializes accepted writes, followers replay its change stream and may serve reads, and failover promotes an eligible follower when the leader is unavailable. Losing the leader stops writes until promotion, while losing one follower mainly reduces read capacity and redundancy.

exercises.prompt: Build the single-leader replication path. A client write must reach the authority, enter one ordered change stream, and then update the read copy.
exercises.why: The leader is the write authority, its replication log fixes one change order, and the follower replays that order to build a readable copy. If the follower stops consuming the log, its applied position falls behind and reads from it become stale; if an asynchronous leader fails before the log record reaches a promotion candidate, that acknowledged write can be lost.

exercises.prompt: Order one asynchronous-replication timeline in which the follower is still behind when the client receives success.
steps: Client sends the write to the leader
Leader records the change in its log
After that acknowledgement, the lagging followers receive and apply the log record
Followers can now serve the new data
exercises.why: The leader records the write before acknowledgement, but asynchronous replication does not require a follower acknowledgement first. This exercise shows the lagging case: followers apply afterward, creating stale-read and failover-loss windows. A fast follower may receive or apply the record before the client gets success; asynchronous replication does not impose an order between those events.

exercises.prompt: The leader can wait for a follower to confirm before telling the client 'done' (synchronous), or reply immediately and let followers catch up (asynchronous). What does synchronous buy and cost?
choices: It's faster and safer — strictly better
The write exists on two machines before you're told it succeeded — but every write now waits for the follower, and if that follower is down, writes stall
It buys nothing; it's a legacy option
exercises.why: Waiting for a follower acknowledgement places the write on a second machine before reporting success, reducing the acknowledged-write loss window. Every write now includes follower network and persistence latency, and writes can stall if the required follower is unavailable unless the system explicitly degrades to asynchronous mode.

exercises.prompt: Why is single-leader replication so common, despite the leader being a bottleneck for writes?
choices: Because one authority orders writes and removes replica-to-replica merge conflicts
It's the only design that exists
exercises.why: Routing writes through one leader establishes one authoritative order, so followers do not merge values accepted independently by writable replicas. Concurrent clients can still cause lost updates or application-level conflicts on the leader; transactions and concurrency control handle those.

exercises.title: Replication lag is the delay before a follower applies a leader's write
exercises.body: With asynchronous replication, the leader may acknowledge a committed write before a follower receives and replays its log record. During that interval, a read sent to the follower returns the state from an earlier log position. The lag ends when replay reaches that write.
exercises.note: Lag grows whenever log generation exceeds transfer or replay capacity. Heavy writes, network loss, slow disks, paused replay, long queries, or maintenance can all create that imbalance.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: Replication lag is the delay before a follower applies a leader's write
exercises.why: With asynchronous replication, the leader may acknowledge a committed write before a follower receives and replays its log record. During that interval, a read sent to the follower returns the state from an earlier log position. The lag ends when replay reaches that write. Lag grows whenever log generation exceeds transfer or replay capacity. Heavy writes, network loss, slow disks, paused replay, long queries, or maintenance can all create that imbalance.

exercises.prompt: A user updates their profile (write goes to the leader), the page reloads, and the read is served by a follower that hasn't caught up yet. What do they see?
choices: Their OLD profile — their own change appears to have vanished
exercises.why: The asynchronous follower has not applied the profile update, so it returns the preceding committed version. Read-your-writes routing sends that user's subsequent reads to the leader or a replica known to have reached the write's log position; failover can still lose the write if no surviving node received it.

exercises.prompt: The delay between a write landing on the leader and appearing on a follower is called replication ______.
exercises.why: Replication lag is the delay or log-position gap between a change on the leader and its application on a follower. During that interval, the follower can return a valid older state.

exercises.prompt: A user refreshes twice. The first read hits a caught-up follower and shows a new comment. The second hits a lagging follower and the comment is gone. What broke?
choices: Monotonic reads — for that user, time appeared to run backwards
exercises.why: Monotonic reads require each later read in a session to reflect at least as recent a state as earlier reads. Load balancing across replicas at different log positions violates that condition. Pinning a session to one advancing replica helps while the pin remains valid; reassignment must account for the last observed position.

exercises.prompt: Which conditions can make follower lag grow? Select all.
choices: The leader generates log records faster than the follower can replay them
Slow follower storage or a paused replay worker
The follower consistently replays faster than logs arrive
exercises.why: Lag grows whenever incoming log work outpaces transfer, persistence, or replay. Heavy leader writes can raise production, while network faults, storage contention, long queries, maintenance, or paused replay can reduce consumption. If replay remains faster than arrival, the follower catches up instead.

exercises.prompt: Which of these genuinely help with replication lag problems? Select all.
choices: Route a user's reads to the leader right after they write
Pin each user to a single replica
Monitor lag and pull badly-lagging replicas out of rotation
exercises.why: Leader routing after a write provides fresher reads, session pinning reduces backward jumps, and lag monitoring can remove replicas that exceed a freshness threshold. An additional follower must consume the same write stream and does not inherently increase apply speed; it helps only if redistributing read load removes resource contention on existing followers.

exercises.prompt: You read from an asynchronous follower. What are you actually getting?
choices: A guarantee the data is current
An answer that's correct as of some moment in the past — possibly right now, possibly seconds ago
An error if it's out of date
exercises.why: An asynchronous follower answers from the latest log position it has applied, which may trail the leader by milliseconds or longer. The application must specify a freshness bound or required log position when an arbitrarily stale committed state is insufficient.

lessons.title: Replication lag is accumulated unapplied work

exercises.title: Lag grows by production rate minus replay rate
exercises.body: A follower receives the leader's log and replays it locally. While the leader produces 5,000 records/sec and replay completes 4,800/sec, the missing 200 records accumulate every second. Catch-up requires replay capacity greater than new log production.
exercises.note: Lag is a queue measured in records, bytes, or time behind the leader.

exercises.prompt: The leader produces 5,000 log records/sec. Each follower apply worker replays 1,200/sec. Over 60 seconds, choose the *fewest* apply workers that prevent lag from growing.
exercises.why: Four workers replay 4,800 records/sec, so lag grows by 200/sec or 12,000 records in one minute. Five replay 6,000/sec, enough to keep up and then consume existing lag when headroom remains.

exercises.title: Failover promotes a replica after the leader is judged unavailable
exercises.body: A failure detector uses missed responses and a timeout to classify the leader as unavailable, then a coordinator promotes an eligible follower. Under asynchronous replication, acknowledged log entries absent from that follower are lost when it becomes the new leader.
exercises.note: A network partition can leave the old leader running. Quorum, leases, or fencing tokens must prevent it from continuing to accept writes after promotion.

exercises.prompt: Your leader dies and you promote a follower. With ASYNCHRONOUS replication, what might be lost?
choices: Any writes the leader had already acknowledged but not yet shipped — those are simply gone
exercises.why: Asynchronous acknowledgement does not require a follower to receive the write. If the leader is permanently lost before shipping it, promotion selects a follower whose log ends earlier, and the previously acknowledged write is absent from the new authoritative history.

exercises.prompt: The leader isn't actually dead — it's just unreachable for 30 seconds. You promote a follower. Then the old leader comes back, still believing it's the leader. What now?
choices: Split brain: two leaders both accepting writes, producing conflicting data with no arbiter
exercises.why: This is split brain: the isolated old leader and promoted follower both accept writes, creating divergent logs. Fencing uses a lease, epoch, storage token, or infrastructure control to make the old leader's writes invalid before the replacement becomes authoritative.

exercises.prompt: So how should you set the failover timeout?
choices: As short as possible — recover fast
As long as possible — never risk a false promotion
You're choosing which mistake to make: too short promotes during a harmless blip (risking split brain), too long leaves you down during a real failure
exercises.why: A short timeout reduces write downtime after a real leader failure but increases false promotion during transient latency, which requires effective fencing to avoid split brain. A long timeout reduces false promotion but extends unavailability when the leader is actually lost.

exercises.prompt: A three-node ledger acknowledges only after the leader and one follower have both flushed a write. The failure target is any one-node crash; correlated loss and operator deletion are outside this policy. Slide toward the replication mode.
exercises.why: Requiring durable acknowledgement from the leader and one follower protects the acknowledged write when either one of those nodes alone crashes, matching the stated scope. It adds network and follower-flush latency and can reduce write availability; correlated loss, bad durability settings, and replicated operator deletion remain outside the guarantee.

exercises.prompt: Why not just let two datacenters each run a leader that accepts writes?
choices: You can — but now two leaders can accept conflicting writes to the same row, and you must decide how to resolve those conflicts
Only one datacenter can hold data
exercises.why: Two regional leaders can accept concurrent writes to the same logical record before replication crosses regions. The system must detect and resolve those conflicts with a domain rule, version ordering, or merge algorithm; otherwise one accepted update may overwrite another.

exercises.prompt: Users report that data they just saved disappears — but only during peak hours. Setup: writes go to the leader, reads are load-balanced across 3 async followers. Diagnosis?
choices: Replication lag under peak write load — reads are landing on followers that are behind. Route reads to the leader for a window after a user writes
exercises.why: Peak writes can make the leader's log advance faster than followers apply it. A reload routed to any of the three followers may therefore read a position before the user's save. Routing post-write reads to the leader or waiting for a replica to reach the write position provides read-your-writes behavior.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of replication?
choices: Replicas make you faster and safer, for free
Copies buy read capacity and survival, and charge you in lag, in writes lost on async failover, and in the risk of split brain
exercises.why: Replicas distribute eligible reads and provide failover candidates. Asynchronous application creates stale-read and acknowledged-write-loss windows, while failover requires failure detection and fencing to prevent split brain. Replication policy chooses these latency, consistency, and availability tradeoffs.

exercises.prompt: An operator changes a feature flag and immediately refreshes, but a read routed to an asynchronous follower shows the old value. What is the direct cause?
choices: The follower has not replayed the acknowledged write yet
exercises.why: Asynchronous followers can serve an earlier log position after the leader acknowledges a write. Read-your-writes requires leader routing, a caught-up position check, or another protocol guarantee.
